report:
# Cranberry Juice/Extract for Preventing Recurrent Cystitis: The Evidence

**Bottom line: Your skepticism is well-supported by current evidence.** The most rigorous, up-to-date research shows cranberry products likely do **not** meaningfully prevent recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs/cystitis) in adult women, despite decades of popular belief.

## Key Evidence

**Cochrane Systematic Review (the gold-standard evidence source):** The Cochrane Database updated its review on cranberries for UTI prevention and concluded that cranberry juice is unlikely to prevent bladder and kidney infections. This overturned an earlier, more favorable Cochrane conclusion, after including more and larger, higher-quality trials that showed minimal or no benefit (https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD004407.pub4/full; summarized at https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2012/10/121016204143.htm).

**Direct comparison trial:** A well-designed double-blind, double-dummy noninferiority trial (Beerepoot et al., *Archives of Internal Medicine*, 2011) randomized 221 premenopausal women with recurrent UTIs to either low-dose antibiotic (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) or cranberry capsules for 12 months. Antibiotics were clearly more effective at preventing recurrences than cranberry capsules — cranberry failed to meet noninferiority criteria (https://www.nutraingredients.com/Article/2011/07/27/Antibiotics-better-for-UTIs-than-cranberry-but-may-increase-drug-resistance-say-researchers/).

**Clinical practice guidance:** Reflecting this evidence, pharmacy/clinical references now note that while cranberry juice has traditionally been recommended, "a Cochrane review found no evidence to support its use for this purpose" (https://www.uspharmacist.com/article/treating-uncomplicated-cystitis-42379).

## Nuance
Some individual trials and meta-analyses have found modest benefits in specific subgroups (e.g., women with very frequent recurrences), and effects seem inconsistent across juice concentration, dose, and adherence — which is likely why earlier smaller studies looked more promising than the larger, more rigorous ones. Overall, though, the weight of evidence does not support cranberry products as a reliable, general prevention strategy.
